card: Paper card. Question: How can a one-dimensional (1D) medium-entropy magnetic alloy be rationally designed to facilitate electromagnetic wave attenuation capability in the low-frequency (2–6 GHz) microwave absorption field?. System: FeCoNi medium-entropy alloy nanoparticles (FeCoNi NP) embedded in a one-dimensional carbon fiber (CF) matrix, specifically FeCoNi/CF-1, FeCoNi/CF-2, and FeCoNi/CF-3; atomic ratios of Fe, Co, and Ni varied (e.g., Fe50Co50, Fe50Co40Ni10, Fe40Co40Ni20).. Processing: FeCoNi NPs synthesized via low-temperature hydrothermal process (120 °C for 12 h) using FeCl2·4H2O, CoCl2·6H2O, NiCl2·6H2O, NaOH, and N2H4·H2O; NPs dispersed in polyacrylonitrile (PAN)/DMF solution; electrospinning at 14.0 kV, 20 cm distance, 0.45 mL h−1; pre-oxidation at 240 °C for 1.5 h followed by 330 °C for 0, 1, or 1.5 h; annealing in H2/Ar (5%) at 700 °C for 2 h with a ramping rate of 5 °C min−1.. Test conditions: Electromagnetic wave absorption performance evaluated via coaxial-line method in the 2–6 GHz frequency range; reflection loss (RL) measured with absorber thickness ranging from 1 to 5 mm; magnetic properties characterized using superconducting quantum interference device magnetometry and vector network analyzer; off-axis electronic holography used to evaluate magnetic field lines.. Findings: The FeCoNi/CF-1 exhibits an effective absorption band (fE) of 1.3 GHz in the low-frequency electromagnetic field at an ultrathin thickness of 2 mm.; The saturation magnetization (Ms) of FeCoNi/CF-1 is 194.0 emu g−1 with a coercivity (Hc) of 107.4 Oe, demonstrating desirable soft ferromagnetic nature.; The average level of imaginary magnetic permeability (μ′′) for FeCoNi/CF-1 is 1.4, significantly higher than the 0.2 limit of most previous literature materials.; The real part of permittivity for FeCoNi/CF-1 is enlarged to 5 times that of pure carbon fibers, while the imaginary part is 3 times higher.; The ID/IG value in Raman spectroscopy for FeCoNi/CF-1 decreased to 1.25 compared to 1.28 for pure CF, indicating increased graphitization.; Magnetic permeability of FeCoNi/CF-2 and FeCoNi/CF-3 exhibited slightly higher values compared to FeCoNi/CF-1, attributed to higher magnetic-carbon ratios.; Magnetic parameters (μ′ and μ′′) reached a maximum range when Ni content was in the middle range (4%–14%).. Mechanism: The enhanced EM wave absorption is attributed to the construction of a one-dimensional magnetic network that increases shape anisotropy and promotes magnetic response, alongside the intrinsic physical features of the medium-entropy alloy which improve magnetic-domain movement. The 1D structure facilitates high-density and continuous magnetic coupling networks where magnetic field lines radiate between adjacent particles, causing frequent domain wall migration and phase lag between internal magnetic moments and external fields. Additionally, the FeCoNi alloy acts as a catalyst for graphitization, enhancing electrical conductivity and dielectric loss, while the medium-entropy design intrinsically upgrades magnetic loss capacity through ferromagnetic resonance and natural loss.. Limitations: The text notes that in the lower-frequency region (2–6 GHz), it is difficult to decouple between impedance matching and EM wave attenuation, which often leads to poor performance in other materials. Furthermore, extending the pre-oxidation time indefinitely causes the carbon content to decrease, leading to a drop in dielectric constant that is not conducive to excellent absorbing properties.. Future work: The study opens up a new method for the design and preparation of high-performance 1D magnetic EM absorbers and suggests that the unique 1D shape can be further applied to other magnetic structures which require good shape anisotropy.. Quote: "The designed one-dimensional FeCoNi/CF exhibits excellent performance, with a broad effective absorption band of 1.3 GHz in the low-frequency electromagnetic field at an ultrathin thickness of 2 mm."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a dual-oxide shell of ZnO/Al2O3 be designed via atomic layer deposition to simultaneously achieve record-high microwave absorption in low-frequency bands and enhanced anti-corrosion properties for FeSiAl alloys?. System: FeSiAl (FSA) core with ZnO and Al2O3 dual-oxide shells (FSA@ZnO@Al2O3), compared to single-shell variants (FSA@ZnO, FSA@Al2O3) and annealed FSA (FSA-500). Processing: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) at 150 °C using N2 carrier gas; ZnO deposited via diethyl zinc (DEZn) and H2O (250 cycles, 0.02 s dose, 8 s purge); Al2O3 deposited via trimethylaluminum (TMA) under identical conditions; followed by annealing at 500 °C under N2 for 2 h. Test conditions: Microwave absorption measured in 0.5–18 GHz frequency range with thicknesses 0.5–5.0 mm; corrosion tests conducted in 5.0 wt% NaCl solution using a three-electrode system (OCP ~1600 s, Tafel scan -500 to 500 mV vs OCP at 1 mV s−1, EIS 10^5 to 10^-2 Hz with 5 mV perturbation). Findings: FSA@ZnO@Al2O3 achieved a minimum reflection loss (RLmin) of -50.6 dB at 3.4 GHz, compared to -13.5 dB for pure FSA.; The effective absorption bandwidth (EAB) of FSA@ZnO@Al2O3 increased up to ~3 times that of pure FSA (1.5 GHz vs 0.5 GHz at ~4.0 GHz).; The anti-corrosion property of the FSA core was improved by 9.0 times compared to bare FSA in 5.0 wt% NaCl solution.; The corrosion rate of FSA@ZnO@Al2O3 decreased by about 9.0 times relative to pristine FSA.; The charge transfer resistance (Rct) and impedance modulus |Z|0.01 Hz of FSA@ZnO@Al2O3 were the highest among all samples.; The corrosion potential (Ecorr) shifted positively to 0.0191 V for FSA@ZnO@Al2O3, compared to -0.1783 V for pure FSA.; The anodic current density of FSA@ZnO@Al2O3 was at least 1.0 order of magnitude lower than that of pure FSA.. Mechanism: Microwave absorption is enhanced by dielectric loss from ZnO/Al2O3 shells (interfacial polarization, Debye relaxation), magnetic loss from the DO3 superlattice structure of the FSA core, improved impedance matching in L/S bands, and high attenuation characteristics. Anti-corrosion is achieved via multistage barriers that obstruct corrosive media (Cl-, H2O, O2) and increase charge transfer resistance, effectively blocking the electric circuit.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The authors propose the FSA@ZnO@Al2O3 gradient structure as a promising platform for the design of next-generation microwave absorbers with improved anti-corrosion properties.. Quote: "The corrosion resistance is improved by the unique multistage oxide barriers."

card: Paper card. Question: How can bulk soft magnetic materials achieve a combination of high strength and good ductility without significantly deteriorating their soft magnetic properties (specifically coercivity)?. System: Non-equiatomic Fe35-x/3Co30-x/3Ni30-x/3Ta5Alx (x = 3, 5, 7 at%) high-entropy alloys, specifically the 7Al-HEA variant with a face-centered cubic matrix and L12 nanoprecipitates.. Processing: As-cast plates (10-mm thick) were hot-rolled at 1473 K to 50% thickness reduction, followed by 10-min homogenization at 1473 K and water quenching.. Test conditions: Tensile testing at room temperature; magnetic properties measured via vibrating sample magnetometry (VSM) and magneto-optical Kerr microscopy; microstructure analyzed via TEM, APT, and 4D-STEM.. Findings: The 7Al-HEA achieved an ultimate tensile strength of 1526 MPa with a tensile elongation of 15.3%.; The yield strength of the 7Al-HEA (1202 MPa) was approximately 245% higher than the base alloy (501 MPa).; The coercivity of the 7Al-HEA was 10.7 Oe, only marginally increased from 8.6 Oe in the 3Al-HEA.; The saturation magnetization (Ms) of the 7Al-HEA was 88 Am2 kg-1, compared to 105 Am2 kg-1 for the 3Al-HEA.; The L12 nanoprecipitates had an average size of 13.5 ± 2.5 nm and a volume fraction greater than 42% in the 7Al-HEA.; Dynamic microband refinement reduced the mean distance between parallel microbands from 735 ± 251 nm to 163 ± 35 nm as local strain increased from 30% to 50%.; The 7Al-HEA maintained 61% of its room temperature Ms value at 773 K.; The lattice strain at the coherent interface varied between -0.2% and 0.5% for the 7Al-HEA.. Mechanism: Strength is enhanced by massive solid solution strengthening, precipitation strengthening via shearing of coherent ordered L12 nanoprecipitates, and dynamic microband refinement. Soft magnetic properties are preserved because the full coherency between the nanoprecipitates and the matrix creates negligible distortion fields, resulting in insignificant pinning of Bloch domain walls compared to grain boundaries.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that conventional strengthening approaches usually significantly deteriorate soft magnetic properties due to Bloch wall interactions with defects.. Future work: The findings provide guidance for developing new high-performance materials with an excellent combination of mechanical and soft magnetic properties as needed for the electrification of transport and industry.. Quote: "Compared to the alloy in precipitate‐free state, the alloy variant with a large volume fraction (>42%) of nanoprecipitates achieves significantly enhanced strength (≈1526 MPa) at good ductility (≈15%), while the coercivity is only marginally increased (<10.7 Oe)."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a multistage mechanical alloying strategy be designed to construct nanocrystalline high-entropy alloys with large aspect ratios and thin intergranular amorphous layers to achieve temperature-stable broadband megahertz electromagnetic wave absorption?. System: FeCoNiCr0.4Cu0.2 high-entropy alloy (HEA) powders. Processing: Multistage mechanical alloying (MMA) consisting of dry milling (0-30 h, argon atmosphere, no process control agent) followed by wet milling (3-10 h, 40 mL anhydrous ethanol). Key parameters: ball-to-powder mass ratio 20:1, large ball (10 mm) to small ball (6 mm) ratio 1:2, 4 min pause every 30 min. Optimal sample D20: 20 h dry milling + 5 h wet milling.. Test conditions: Electromagnetic properties measured at -50 to 150 °C in the MHz frequency range; Corrosion resistance tested in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution; Magnetic properties (VSM) measured from 30 to 840 °C; Reflection loss calculated for D20/SiO2 composites (8:2 mass ratio) with thicknesses of 1-5 mm.. Findings: The D20 sample (20 h dry + 5 h wet) achieved a single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) structure with high crystallinity.; The average intergranular amorphous layer thickness of the D20 sample was less than 2 nm.; The D20 sample exhibited a Curie temperature of 774 °C.; The maximum reflection loss (RL) of D20/SiO2 composites (8:2 mass ratio, 5 mm thickness) was greater than -7 dB.; The electromagnetic wave absorption bandwidth (RL < -7 dB) maintained between 523 and 600 MHz from -50 to 150 °C.; The corrosion current density (icorr) of the D20 sample was 7.0 μA cm−2.; The charge transfer resistance (Rct) of the D20 sample was 3,739 Ω in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.; The D20 sample showed a smaller permeability temperature coefficient compared to samples with different milling times.. Mechanism: The phase transition from BCC to amorphous to FCC occurs primarily during dry milling, with the FCC phase providing superior ductility for flattening during wet milling. The resulting large aspect ratios break the Snoek's limit and enhance planar anisotropy, while the thin intergranular amorphous layers (<2 nm) facilitate strong magnetic coupling between nanograins, leading to high and temperature-stable permeability. The 'cocktail effect' of the HEA elements contributes to high corrosion resistance and high Curie temperature.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that excessive wet milling time leads to serious crushing of particles and that high temperatures (150 °C) can cause a slight decrease in absorption performance due to increased permittivity affecting impedance matching.. Future work: The authors state the work provides a facile and tunable strategy to design MHz electromagnetic absorbers with temperature stability, broadband, and resistance to harsh environments, implying future application in such environments, but do not explicitly list specific future research directions beyond the general utility of the strategy.. Quote: "FeCoNiCr0.4Cu0.2 HEAs with dry milling 20 h and wet milling 5 h (D20) exhibit higher and more stable permeability because of larger aspect ratios and thinner intergranular amorphous layers."

card: Paper card. Question: Why does the CoCrFeMnNi equiatomic high-entropy alloy fail to form stacking fault tetrahedra (SFTs) or vacancy clusters during high-speed plastic deformation and subsequent annealing, despite having a low stacking fault energy similar to metals where SFTs typically form?. System: CoCrFeMnNi equiatomic high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Vacuum induction furnace fabrication; homogenization at 1473 K for 10 h; rolling to ~50 µm; annealing at 1273 K for 1 h in 10⁻⁵ Pa vacuum; high-speed tearing at 1 m/s (strain rate ~10⁶/s); isochronal annealing from room temperature to 873 K in 100 K increments for 10 min.. Test conditions: Dark-field weak-beam transmission electron microscopy (TEM) along [011] direction with g = 200; annealing temperatures up to 873 K; high-speed deformation at ~10⁶/s strain rate.. Findings: No stacking fault tetrahedra (SFTs) were observed in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA after high-speed deformation or after annealing at 873 K.; The average binding energy of di-vacancy clusters was positive (0.25 eV), indicating a tendency to form.; The average binding energy of tri-vacancy clusters was negative (-0.44 eV), ranging between -0.48 and -0.35 eV, indicating instability.; Binding energies for tetra-vacancy clusters were calculated to be positive, suggesting they can be stable.; In contrast, Ni and Cu showed positive binding energies for di-, tri-, and tetra-vacancy clusters that increased with cluster size.; The inability to form tri-vacancy clusters suppresses defect accumulation and promotes interstitial-vacancy recombination.; Under cascade damage (ion/neutron irradiation), tetra-vacancy clusters can form directly, but growth from excess vacancies is suppressed.. Mechanism: The instability of tri-vacancy clusters (negative binding energy) prevents the formation of larger vacancy clusters (like SFTs) under conditions without cascade damage (e.g., high-speed deformation). This is attributed to lattice distortion caused by the random occupation of lattice sites by atoms of different sizes (Co/Ni undersized, Cr/Fe/Mn oversized). While tri-vacancy clusters are unstable, tetra-vacancy clusters become stable due to the relaxation of this lattice distortion, allowing them to form only under high-energy cascade damage conditions.. Limitations: The authors state that there are no reliable experimental data to support the calculated migration energy of single vacancies (0.79 ± 0.12 eV). They also note that the surface of the annealed sample was slightly oxidized, making dark-field weak-beam images unclear. Additionally, the study does not fully explain why tetra-vacancy clusters are stable while tri-vacancy clusters are unstable, calling for further detailed analysis.. Future work: It is necessary to analyze in detail why the tetra-vacancy cluster is stable while the tri-vacancy cluster is unstable. The authors also state that the same calculations regarding cascade damage are required for the CoCrFeMnNi HEA, as previous simulations were only done for CoCrFeNi HEA.. Quote: "The binding energy of the di-vacancy cluster was positive (average of 0.25 eV), while that of the tri-vacancy cluster was negative (average of − 0.44 eV)"

W3001455898.title: Chemical environment and magnetic moment effects on point defect formations in CoCrNi-based concentrated solid-solution alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How does chemical complexity in single-phase concentrated solid solution alloys (SP-CSAs) affect the migration range and evolution of radiation-induced defects compared to pure nickel under ion irradiation?. System: Single crystalline pure nickel (Ni), 50%Ni50%Co (NiCo), and 50%Ni50%Fe (NiFe) with fcc structure. Processing: Ion beam irradiation using 3 MeV Au ions at room temperature to fluences of 2 × 10^13/cm^2, ~1 × 10^14/cm^2, and ~5 × 10^15/cm^2; samples prepared via FIB lift-out followed by flash polishing (4% perchloric acid in 96% ethanol, 6~14 V, -30 to -50 °C, 0.05-0.2 s). Test conditions: Room temperature irradiation; cross-sectional TEM (300 keV, g=[200]), RBS-C (3.5 MeV He+ ions), k-ART simulations (300 K and 900 K), and MD simulations (40 keV PKA). Findings: Defect clusters in pure Ni stretched to 550 nm at 2 × 10^13/cm^2 and ~1,100 nm at 5 × 10^15/cm^2, exceeding SRIM predictions.; Defect clusters in NiCo and NiFe reached ~460 nm and ~460 nm respectively at low fluence, and ~900 nm and ~800 nm at high fluence.; The damage range in pure Ni was significantly deeper than in NiCo and NiFe at high fluence, indicating higher defect migration rates in pure Ni.; Vacancy-type stacking fault tetrahedra (SFT) and interstitial loops coexist in the same region, consistent with MD simulations.; k-ART simulations showed small vacancy clusters (di-vacancies, tri-vacancies) have migration barriers of 0.3–0.4 eV, making them highly mobile at room temperature.; RBS-C measurements showed damage ranges slightly shallower than TEM (e.g., NiCo: 350 nm vs 460 nm at low fluence) due to density assumptions.; High-fluence irradiation (1.1 × 10^17/cm^2) induced high-level mechanical stress, with implanted Au atoms occupying lattice sites (~7% concentration).. Mechanism: The extended damage range beyond the theoretical ion stopping depth is attributed to the migration of highly mobile small vacancy clusters and interstitials, prolonged irradiation time allowing further diffusion, and mechanical stress gradients from implanted Au ions driving defects deeper. The slower migration in alloys is caused by higher defect migration barriers due to intrinsic chemical disorder and lattice distortion, which localize energy dissipation and enhance defect recombination.. Limitations: The text notes that RBS-C depth calculations assume un-irradiated sample density, ignoring potential irradiation-induced volume swelling, and that the 'knee' point method for determining damage range relies on assumptions that may not align perfectly with TEM criteria.. Future work: The authors propose that the chemical species of SP-CSA alloys on defect migration should be studied in further detail, particularly by computer simulation.. Quote: "Defects in nickel migrate faster than in NiCo and NiFe."

card: Paper card. Question: How can a unique five-element Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn high entropy alloy thin film be synthesized in a single step to achieve soft magnetic properties with high saturation magnetization and low coercivity, overcoming the challenges of anomalous deposition and phase control in aqueous media?. System: Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn high entropy alloy (near equi-atomic composition). Processing: Pulse electrodeposition in aqueous medium at ~45 ºC; optimized parameters: forward ON time 50 ms, OFF time 10 ms, applied potential 1.5 V (potentiostatic mode), using sodium citrate as complexing agent and boric acid as buffer.. Test conditions: Room temperature characterization; Magnetic properties measured via Vibrating Sample Magnetometry (VSM) and Ferromagnetic Resonance (FMR) from 9 to 18 GHz; Microstructure analyzed via FESEM, STEM-EDS, 2D X-ray diffraction, and HRTEM.. Findings: The fabricated Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn HEA thin films exhibited a saturation magnetization (Ms) of ~82 emu/g.; The films showed a relatively low coercivity (Hc) of 19.5 Oe and a remanent magnetization (Mr) of 1.17%.; The alloy hosts nanocrystalline features with a grain size ranging from ~5 to 20 nm.; The films possess a dual-phase structure consisting of Face Centered Cubic (FCC) and Body Centered Cubic (BCC) phases.; FMR measurements yielded a 4πMs value of ~16,136 Oe, indicating potential for microwave device applications.; The composition was found to be uniform throughout the film with no different chemical compositions in FCC and BCC grains.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the soft magnetic behavior and high saturation magnetization to the crystalline nature of the films (FCC/BCC dual phases) and the high concentration of ferromagnetic elements (Fe, Co, Ni) relative to diamagnetic elements (Cu, Zn). The pulse electrodeposition technique controls the reduction of five metal ions uniformly by managing the local pH, minimizing hydroxide formation, and reducing residual stresses, which facilitates the formation of nanocrystalline grains and twins with low stacking fault energy.. Limitations: The text notes that the composition of the HEA thin films varies slightly between STEM-EDS (single location) and FESEM-EDS (multiple locations) due to local heterogeneities and length scale differences, though the overall distribution is confirmed to be within the HEA range.. Future work: The authors propose that additional tuning of the electrodeposition parameters and the relative composition of the constituent elements can further reduce the coercivity of the thin film.. Quote: "The fabricated Co–Cu–Fe–Ni–Zn HEA thin films exhibited high saturation magnetization value of ~ 82 emu/g, relatively low coercivity value of 19.5 Oe and remanent magnetization of 1.17%."

W569457833.title: Electrodeposition of Alloys: PRINCIPLES and PRACTICE

card: Paper card. Question: How can the strength–ductility trade-off inherent to traditional alloys be overcome in multi-principal-element alloys by exploiting multiple levels of heterogeneities?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) and medium-entropy alloys (MEAs) including FCC-based systems (e.g., CoCrFeNi, CrCoNi, VCoNi), BCC-based refractory systems (e.g., TiZrHfNbTa), dual-phase eutectic lamella HEAs, and alloys with multicomponent intermetallic nanoparticles (MCINPs). Processing: Partial recrystallization to create heterogeneous grain structures (HGS), spinodal decomposition to form precipitates, addition of oxygen solutes (~2 at%) to form nanoscale complexes, and intentional alloying to tune stacking fault energy (SFE) for deformation-induced transformations. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) uniaxial tensile testing; cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K) for specific FCC MEAs; compression testing for some refractory BCC HEAs. Findings: An FCC-MCINP alloy achieved a yield strength above 1 GPa with a uniform elongation (εu) of ~50%, showing no strength–ductility trade-off compared to unstrengthened elemental metals.; A single-phase CrCoNi MEA with a heterogeneous grain structure (HGS) spanning nano-to-micro scales reached a gigapascal yield strength while maintaining εu in excess of 20%.; The VCoNi MEA achieved near-GPa yield strength with εu ~30% and total elongation ~38%, attributed to maximized lattice friction from atomic size mismatch.; In BCC-TiZrHfNb HEA, adding ~2 at% oxygen formed nanoscale (O, Ti, Zr)-complexes that increased tensile elongation from ~14% to ~28% while maintaining high strength.; Stress-assisted martensitic transformation in BCC-Ti35Zr27.5Hf27.5Nb5Ta5 HEA created a 65% volume fraction of internally twinned martensite, doubling the strain-hardening rate.; Wide hysteresis loops in load–unload–reload stress–strain curves demonstrated that nonhomogeneous plastic deformation in HGS alloys imparts high back stresses contributing to strain hardening.; At cryogenic temperatures (77 K and 4 K), the CrCoNi MEA exhibited strain-hardening rates and εu comparable to the best 316 austenitic stainless steels due to reduced dynamic recovery.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the high concentration of multiple principal elements creates a rugged energy landscape with statistical fluctuations in composition and local chemical order (LCO), causing dislocations to adopt a wavy line and face intermittent 'nanoscale segment detrapping' barriers. This intrinsic lattice friction is compounded by a hierarchy of heterogeneities (defects, precipitates, grain boundaries, phase boundaries) that promote nonhomogeneous plastic deformation, geometrically necessary dislocation storage, and dynamic mechanisms like twinning (TWIP) and transformation (TRIP), which sustain high strain-hardening rates to delay necking.. Limitations: Refractory BCC HEAs often lack room-temperature tensile ductility due to a drastic rise in the ductile-to-brittle transition temperature; TRIP-assisted DP alloys with low initial yield strength require hardening (e.g., cold work) which causes the strain-hardening rate to become inadequate, restoring the strength–ductility trade-off at high σy levels.. Future work: Continued endeavors to tailor heterogeneities to ward off plastic instabilities and realize even better strength–ductility balance, expanding the repertoire of alloys in compositions and properties through refined and enhanced HEAs.. Quote: "The strength of HEAs is considerably higher than traditional solid solutions, as the many constituents lead to a rugged energy landscape that increases the resistance to dislocation motion."

card: Paper card. Question: How does a Permanent Parallel Magnetic Field (PPMF) of 9 T affect the electrodeposition current, mass deposition, and surface morphology of Ni-Co-Fe-Zn quaternary alloys compared to deposition without a magnetic field?. System: Ni-Co-Fe-Zn quaternary alloys deposited from a chloride solution containing 1 M NiCl2·6H2O, 0.25 M CoCl2·6H2O, 0.25 M FeCl2·4H2O, 0.25 M ZnCl2, and 0.5 M H3BO3. Processing: Electrodeposition via chronoamperometry and cyclic voltammetry at -1.1, -1.2, and -1.3 V for 2400 seconds at 30-32°C and pH 4 ± 0.1, with and without a 9 T Permanent Parallel Magnetic Field (PPMF) applied parallel to the cathode surface. Test conditions: Temperature: 30-32°C; pH: 4 ± 0.1; Electrolyte: Chloride bath; Magnetic field: 9 T PPMF parallel to cathode; Duration: 2400 sec; Potentials: -1.1, -1.2, -1.3 V. Findings: The percentage of current enhancement (Γ%) increased with more negative potentials: 11.9% at -1.1 V, 16.7% at -1.2 V, and 18.5% at -1.3 V for a 2400 sec duration.; Surface roughness (RMS) decreased from 48.5 nm to 23 nm at -1.1 V and from 112 nm to 39 nm at -1.3 V when the PPMF was applied.; The limiting current was enhanced in the presence of the PPMF, with current values increasing from 6.7 to 7.5 mA at -1.1 V, 18 to 20 mA at -1.2 V, and 27 to 32 mA at -1.3 V.; The mass of electrodeposition increased with the presence of the PPMF, with the difference in mass deposition ranging from 0.03 to 0.107 mg cm min-1.; The Content of Ni in the electrodeposited layers was always lower than the Composition Reference Line (CRL) due to anomalous behavior.; The lowest elemental content in the deposited layers belonged to Fe due to the chemical oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+ in the solution.; The morphology changed from polyhedral grains (without PPMF) to a nodular shape (with PPMF) at -1.10 V.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the increased mass transport and current to the Magneto-Hydrodynamic (MHD) effect, largely caused by the Lorentz Force, which reduces the diffusion layer thickness. They also suggest that the magnetic field suppresses dendritic growth by reducing the effective potential at the tips of dendrites, leading to smoother surfaces.. Limitations: The text notes that the solution was free of chelating reagents, which led to the lowest elemental content being Fe due to oxidation of Fe2+ to Fe3+, and states that the smoothness effect of an applied magnetic field on electrodeposition surfaces is still unclear.. Quote: "The percentage of current enhancement (Γ%) was increased in the presence of PPMF, with results of Γ% = 11.9%, 16.7% and 18.5% at -1.1, -1.2 and -1.3 V respectively for a 2400 sec duration."

card: Paper card. Question: How does deep multi-element co-substitution of Fe3+ cations with Al3+, Co3+, Cr3+, Ga3+, and In3+ affect the phase stability, crystal structure, and magnetic properties of SrFe12O19 hexaferrites?. System: SrFe12O19 hexaferrite deeply substituted up to at.67% by Al3+, Co3+, Cr3+, Ga3+, and In3+ cations (samples A1–A6 identified as single-phase). Processing: Conventional solid-phase synthesis: mixing Fe2O3, Ga2O3, Al2O3, Cr2O3, In2O3, CoO, and SrCO3; hand grinding in agate mortar for 30 min; planetary milling for 6 h; pressing at 5 tons force (8×5 mm cylinders); sintering at 1400°C for 5 h on platinum substrate under alundum crucible. Test conditions: XRD (5°–90°, Cu-Kα, room temperature); SQUID magnetometry (field up to 16 kOe at 300 K; temperature up to 400 K in 1.6 kOe; ZFC/FC in 300 Oe). Findings: Six single-phase samples (A1–A6) were obtained, while others formed non-single-phase products.; Unit cell volume varied from V ≈ 648.21(17) Å³ (sample A6) to V ≈ 694.13(18) Å³ (sample A4).; Average grain size ranged from 2 to 5 μm, with porosity not exceeding ~4%.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) at 300 K ranged from ~1 emu/g (A6) to ~5 emu/g (A4), with a maximum of Ms ≈ 43 emu/g recorded for A5 at 100 K.; Magnetic ordering temperature (Tmo) varied from ~80 K (A6 in 1.6 kOe) to ~381.8 K (A3 in 1.6 kOe).; Freezing temperature (Tf) ranged from ~77 K (A5) to ~341 K (A3).; Average magnetic cluster size was estimated at ~350–400 nm.; All magnetization curves were nonmonotonic with respect to the average ionic radius ⟨rM⟩.. Mechanism: Deep co-substitution leads to magnetic dilution and inhomogeneous distribution of cations, which weakens the Fe3+(M3+)–O2−–Fe3+(M3+) indirect superexchange interactions despite some reduction in bond lengths, resulting in a frustrated magnetic state composed of magnetically disordered nanosized clusters within a magnetically ordered matrix.. Limitations: The study relied solely on XRD for structural analysis, which provides only average behavior; detailed local structure and cation distribution require Mössbauer spectroscopy and neutron diffraction. Additionally, only the cheapest solid-phase method was used without optimizing annealing, cooling rates, or pressure.. Future work: The authors plan to perform Mössbauer spectroscopy and powder neutron diffraction to determine the exact distribution of substituting cations over nonequivalent crystallographic positions and to refine the understanding of exchange interactions.. Quote: "Deep co-substitution of the Fe3+ iron cations in SrFe12O19 strontium hexaferrite with M3+ triply charged diamagnetic Al3+, Ga3+, and In3+, as well as paramagnetic Co3+, and Cr3+ cations leads to a weakening of the Fe3+(M3+) – O2− – Fe3+(M3+) indirect superexchange and forms the frustrated magnetic state"

card: Paper card. Question: Why do tri- and pentachromium(II) extended metal atom chains exhibit similar magnetic anisotropy and single-molecule magnet behavior despite having different structural preferences (symmetric vs. unsymmetric) and electronic structures?. System: [Cr3(dpa)4X2] (X = Cl–, SCN–) and [Cr5(tpda)4X2] (X = Cl–, SCN–). Processing: Synthesis via ligand exchange: [Cr3(dpa)4Cl2] reacted with TlBF4 in CH3CN followed by KSCN addition to yield [Cr3(dpa)4(NCS)2]; pentachromium complexes prepared by literature procedures; single crystals grown by layering solutions with n-hexane.. Test conditions: dc/ac magnetic susceptibility (1.8–320 K, 0–70 kOe), W-band EPR (94 GHz, 100 K), high-frequency EPR (220.8 and 331.2 GHz), DFT/CASSCF calculations on gas-phase structures.. Findings: All four complexes exhibit easy-axis anisotropy with |D| = 1.5–1.8 cm–1 in their S = 2 ground state.; Pentachromium(II) species adopt an unsymmetric structure with alternating short (1.86–2.07 Å) and long (2.50–2.66 Å) Cr–Cr distances, while trichromium(II) species are symmetric.; In pentachromium(II) species, four unpaired electrons are largely localized on the terminal, 'isolated' Cr2+ ion.; In trichromium(II) species, four unpaired electrons occupy nonbonding combinations of 3d-like orbitals centered on the two terminal metals.; Energy barriers for magnetic relaxation (Ueff) are 10.6(6) K for [Cr3(dpa)4Cl2] and 8.6(5) K for [Cr5(tpda)4Cl2].; The extent of unpaired-electron delocalization has little impact on the magnetic anisotropy of these wire-like molecular species.; The larger |D| value in isothiocyanato derivatives compared to chlorido derivatives is predicted by AOM and confirmed by CASSCF calculations.. Mechanism: The similar magnetic anisotropy arises because the QRO eigenvalues closely mirror the 3d-level pattern of the terminal ions in both symmetric and unsymmetric structures. In both cases, the terminal ions have a similar coordination environment (square-pyramidal or vacant-octahedral), and the key factor is the similar pattern of molecular orbitals coupled by spin–orbit interaction, rather than the degree of spin delocalization along the chain.. Limitations: The study notes that post-HF methods (CASSCF) could only be applied to truncated subunits (monomer and dimer) due to hardware computational limits, preventing full system calculation for the pentachromium species.. Future work: The authors state that the findings shed new light on the controversy concerning spin delocalization, implying further investigation into the role of thermal energy and crystal packing on molecular geometry in these systems.. Quote: "We conclude that the extent of unpaired-electron delocalization has little impact on the magnetic anisotropy of these wire-like molecular species."

Paper card. Question: How do symmetric (n=3) versus unsymmetric (n=5) structural preferences in chromium(II)-based extended metal atom chains (EMACs) influence the distribution of unpaired electrons and the zero-field splitting (zfs) parameter D, and why do both systems exhibit similar magnetic anisotropy despite different structural motifs?. System: Chromium(II)-based extended metal atom chains (EMACs) with odd-membered chains (n=3 and n=5), specifically complexes with axial ligands X = Cl– and SCN– (e.g., 1asym, 1bsym, 2aunsym, 2bunsym). Processing: Synthesis of tri- and pentachromium(II) complexes; DFT/PBE calculations for electronic structure and QROs; CASSCF(8,8) calculations for Cr2–Cr3 fragments and terminal Cr1 chromophores; Quasi-restricted DFT approach (Neese et al.) for zfs parameter estimation; Zn2+ substitution modeling (Cr1Zn4) to isolate fragment effects. Test conditions: Computational analysis at CASSCF and DFT levels; comparison of symmetric (D4) and unsymmetric (C4) structures; evaluation of axial ligand effects (Cl– vs SCN–); calculation of D, E, and |E/D| parameters for S=2 ground states. Findings: Both tri- and pentachromium(II) strings exhibit a negative zfs parameter D with |D| = 1.5–1.8 cm–1 and weak rhombicity (|E/D| ≤ 0.02).; The Cr2–Cr3 unit in unsymmetric pentachromium chains is a diamagnetic fragment with a singlet ground state more stable by 3927.95 cm–1.; UNO analysis of the Cr2–Cr3 singlet ground state yields a bond order of 2.27, deviating from the expected value of 4 due to partial occupation of antibonding orbitals.; Zn2+ substitution (Cr1Zn4 model) shows that diamagnetic substitution has a limited impact on calculated D values, which become somewhat less negative.; Spin-forbidden (α → β) ligand field excitations contribute significantly to the D parameter and cannot be neglected.; In symmetric trichromium chains, the four SOMOs are nonbonding linear combinations of d orbitals centered on terminal metals (Cr1 and Cr3) with no contribution from Cr2.; Isothiocyanato derivatives display slightly higher magnetic anisotropy compared to chlorido complexes.; The D parameter is expected to be negative and of similar magnitude in both tri- and pentachromium(II) species despite different electron delocalization patterns.. Mechanism: In unsymmetric pentachromium chains, the terminal Cr1 ion is structurally isolated, and its d orbitals provide the leading contribution to the four SOMOs. In symmetric trichromium chains, although terminal metals are equivalent, the four SOMOs are nonbonding linear combinations of d orbitals on terminal metals (Cr1 and Cr3), with energies mirroring the LF-split d orbitals of terminal ions. The similar energy patterns of frontier orbitals in both systems result in comparable magnetic anisotropy, while axial ligands exert a small but detectable influence on the D parameter through changes in ligand field strength.. Limitations: CASSCF calculations cannot be applied to the symmetric structure of trichromium(II) complexes due to the unmanageable computational resources required to extend the CAS space over the 3d sets of three Cr2+ ions. The D parameter values obtained are only semiquantitative because several other excitations involving doubly occupied and empty orbitals, as well as spin–spin contributions, were not included.. Future work: A series of Cr3 compounds with a variety of axial ligands is currently under examination to confirm the degree of their influence on the magnitude of the relaxation barrier, specifically comparing complexes with strong (e.g., CN–) and weak (e.g., BF4–) donors.. Quote: "The singlet state was found more stable by 3927.95 cm–1, indicating that the Cr2–Cr3 unit can be regarded as a diamagnetic fragment."

Question: How does the partial substitution of non-magnetic Mg2+ with magnetic Co2+ in Y-type Ba2Mg2Fe12O22 hexaferrites affect the crystal structure, iron oxidation state, and magnetic phase transition temperatures?. System: Ba2Mg0.4Co1.6Fe12O22 (Y-type hexaferrite family Ba2Me2Fe12O22). Processing: Sonochemical co-precipitation: metal nitrates dissolved in deionized water with 10 wt% over-stoichiometric Ba(NO3)2, precipitated with NaOH at pH = 11.5, sonicated with 750 W ultrasound (40% amplitude) for 15 min, dried, milled, calcined at 700 °C, and heat-treated at 1170 °C for 7 hours in air.. Test conditions: XRD at ambient temperature (40 kV, 30 mA, Cu-Kα); Mössbauer spectroscopy at room temperature (±12 mm/s velocity range); Magnetization measurements at 4.2 K and 300 K up to 50 kOe; ZFC/FC curves in fields of 50, 100, 500, and 1000 Oe from 4.2 to 300 K.. Findings: The material is an almost pure Y-type hexaferrite phase with only 1.4% CoFe2O4 impurity.; Unit cell parameters remained unchanged compared to unsubstituted Ba2Mg2Fe12O22 (a = 5.8613(1) Å, c = 43.503(1) Å).; Isomer shifts of 0.27–0.38 mm/s confirm high-spin Fe3+ with no ferrous Fe2+ observed.; Magnetization at 50 kOe increased to 34.5 emu/g at 4.2 K and 30.5 emu/g at 300 K.; Two magnetic phase transitions were observed, both shifted to higher temperatures compared to the undoped compound.; The ferrimagnetic-to-helical spin order transition occurs at approximately 195 K (depending on field).; A second transition to a longitudinal-conical spin state was determined at 85 K (at 500 Oe).; The coercive field at 300 K was found to be about 35 Oe.. Mechanism: The substitution of Mg2+ by Co2+ in octahedral sites does not alter the iron oxidation state but modifies the magnetic anisotropy, which is temperature and field-dependent, thereby shifting the magnetic phase transition temperatures to higher values and increasing saturation magnetization.. Limitations: The authors state that the reason for the decrease in the second transition temperature to 78 K at 1 kOe is still unknown.. Future work: The authors propose future studies using structure-sensitive methods, including neutron diffraction, combined with other advanced techniques to prove multiferroicity, especially given the transition temperatures are now above liquid nitrogen temperature.. Quote: "The magnetization values at 50 kOe were 34.5 emu/g at 4.2 K and 30.5 emu/g at 300 K."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the structural tunability of high-entropy materials (HEMs), specifically the antisite disordering and lattice distortion, be leveraged to optimize catalytic performance and energy storage capabilities compared to traditional alloys or compounds?. System: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) such as PtPdRhRuCe, CoMoFeNiCu, AlNiCoFeX; High-entropy oxides (HEOs) such as (MgCoNiCuZn)Ox, (CoCuMgNiZn)Ox, Li-containing entropy-stabilized oxyfluorides; High-entropy metallic glasses (HEMGs); High-entropy borides (HEBs), carbides (HECs), sulfides (HESs), and nitrides (HENs). Processing: Synthesis methods include carbothermal shock (CTS) with thermal shock at ~2,000 K within 55 ms; fast-moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) heating to ~923 K within 5 s; ultrasonication-assisted wet-chemistry with local temperatures up to ~5,000°C; electrodeposition confining precursors to water nanodroplets within 100 ms; solid-state sintering; solvothermal synthesis; and mechanochemical methods. Test conditions: Catalysis tested at temperatures up to 1500 K and reaction temperatures of 305 °C or 155 °C for CO oxidation; electrocatalysis performed at ~80 °C in acidic and basic electrolytes; battery cycling at rates up to 2000 mA/g; supercapacitor testing in 1 m KOH solution at 100 mV/s scan rate. Findings: PtPdRhRuCe NPs achieved ~100% conversion and >99% nitrogen oxide selectivity for ammonia oxidation with no activity degradation.; Quinary CoMoFeNiCu NPs on carbon nanofiber showed a more than 20 times improvement in NH3 conversion rate versus Ru catalysts.; Co0.2Ni0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Zn0.2O HEO achieved 98% conversion of benzyl alcohol in only 2 h under solvent-free aerobic oxidation.; Ni20Fe20Mo10Co35Cr15 HEA catalyst exhibited an overpotential of 107 mV in acidic solutions, comparable to Pt sheet.; Nanoporous AlCuNiPtMn exhibited a half-wave potential of 0.945 V in acidic media, representing a ~16-fold mass activity of Pt/C for ORR.; AuAgPtPdCu HEA catalyst achieved a faradaic efficiency of about 100% toward gaseous products at -0.3 V for CO2 reduction.; Rock-salt (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O anode delivered an initial capacity of 446 mAh/g and 256 mAh/g after 100 cycles in a full cell.; Nanoporous AlCoCrFeNi HEA exhibited a high volumetric capacitance of 700 F/cm3 and excellent cycling stability of over 3,000 cycles.. Mechanism: The authors attribute enhanced performance to the 'high-entropy effect', 'lattice distortion effect', 'sluggish diffusion effect', and 'cocktail effect', which stabilize single-phase solid solutions and create diverse local electronic structures and adsorption energies. The large number of atomic sites allows tuning of surface electronic structures and adsorption energies, while the uniform configuration leads to severe lattice distortion that increases the activation barrier of diffusion, improving kinetic stability.. Limitations: The fundamental correlations between compositions and phases (e.g., phase diagrams) are not clear; the surface structures of HEMs may not be preserved at working conditions; productivity of HEA NPs via CTS is very low; the actual contribution of entropy versus enthalpy to Gibbs free energy is difficult to determine; and the surface structure of HEMs is more complicated than current catalysts.. Future work: Future work includes enhancing productivity for industrial applications, developing theoretical investigations using DFT and machine learning to design proper HEMs, achieving precise structural control of size, shape, and composition, developing 3D characterization techniques like electron tomography and APT, and exploring new types of HEMs with more than five elements.. Quote: "Precursor of metal salt mixtures was thermally shocked at ~ 2,000 K within 55 ms (as shown in Figure 2A), alloying up to eight dissimilar elements into single-phase solid-solution NPs"

Question: How does the addition of Sn (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10) affect the phase constitution, microstructure, and magnetic properties (specifically saturation magnetization, remanence, and Curie temperature) of FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8 high-entropy alloys?. System: FeCoNi(CuAl)0.8Snx (0 ≤ x ≤ 0.10). Processing: Vacuum arc-melting of 99.99% purity constituent elements using a water-cooled Cu crucible, followed by suction casting into a 100 × 10× 2 mm water-cooled Cu mold after remelting four times.. Test conditions: XRD scan speed of 1°/min; VSM measurements at an applied magnetic field of 1 T; HCTS hysteresis curves using a 27 × 9 × 1.7 mm rectangular sample at a magnetic field of 25 kA/m; DSC thermal stability analysis at a heating rate of 10 K/min.. Findings: The ratio of I(110)BCC/I(111)FCC increases from 0.38 (x=0) to 10.53 (x=0.10), indicating a rapid increase in BCC phase content.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) increases from 78.6 Am2/kg to 88.8 Am2/kg as x increases from 0 to 0.10, an increase of almost 13 percent.; The Curie temperature of the FCC phase increases significantly, reaching 634.9 K for x = 0.04.; Remanence (Br) decreases after the addition of Sn, which is different from the effect of Ga addition.; The average size of nanoscale precipitates in the BCC matrix changes from 20 ± 5 nm (rod-like) in the Sn-free alloy to approximately 100 nm length and 30 nm width in the x=0.10 alloy.; A phase transformation from FCC to BCC occurs at temperatures between 600–700 K, causing magnetization to increase in this range.; Unknown phases appear in XRD patterns for x ≥ 0.02, which are inferred to be rich in Cu, Ni, and Sn.. Mechanism: The addition of Sn promotes the formation of the BCC phase, which has a higher Curie temperature and higher saturation magnetization than the FCC phase. The increase in magnetization at high temperatures (600–700 K) is attributed to the transformation of the FCC phase (low Tc) to the BCC phase (high Tc). The shape change of Cu-rich nano-precipitates is due to the segregation of Cu and Sn in the phase boundary regions and the decrease of Cu solubility in the BCC phase.. Limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.08, only a small number of FCC phase transform to BCC phase, limiting the magnetization increase at higher temperatures. Additionally, unknown phases appear in the XRD patterns for x ≥ 0.02, the composition of which is only partially deduced.. Future work: The authors propose that these alloys can be used as new soft magnetic materials at high temperatures and suggest the work provides a new idea for designing future high-performance soft magnetic materials.. Quote: "The addition of Sn promotes the formation of BCC phase, and it also affects the shape of Cu-rich nano-precipitates in BCC matrix."

Question: How can High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) be designed and optimized to simultaneously achieve high saturation magnetization, high electrical resistivity, and high malleability for soft magnetic material applications?. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8). Processing: Arc-melting pure elements (>99.5 wt.% purity) in high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth, remelted four times for homogeneity; rapid solidification into ingots; compressive testing of cylindrical samples (Φ3 × 6 mm) at room temperature with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing; X-ray diffraction (30 kV, 20 mA, Cu target, 10°/min); Electrical resistivity measurement; Magnetization curves via Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS); SEM-EDS microstructural analysis. Findings: The optimal balance of properties is achieved at x = 0.2 (A2 alloy) with saturation magnetization of 1.15 T, coercivity of 1,400 A/m, electrical resistivity of 69.5 μΩ·cm, yield strength of 342 MPa, and strain without fracture of 50%.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) drops almost monotonically from 1.315 T at x = 0 (A0) to 0.46 T at x = 0.8 (A8) upon Al and Si addition.; Alloys with x ≤ 0.2 exhibit a single-phase FCC solid solution, while x = 0.3 shows a BCC + FCC mixture, and x ≥ 0.4 transitions to almost entirely BCC structure.; Plastic deformation (εp) exceeds 50% without fracture for x in the range of 0 to 0.2, whereas ductility diminishes significantly for x ≥ 0.4, with A8 shattering immediately after elastic deformation.; Electrical resistivity generally increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8, reaching 69.5 μΩ·cm at x = 0.2, which falls within the typical range (50–80 μΩ·cm) of silicon steels.; The A3 alloy (x = 0.3) exhibits a yield strength of 938 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 2,857 MPa with 33% plasticity, attributed to the mixture of FCC and BCC phases.; Coercivity (Hc) is low for x ≤ 0.2 but increases dramatically at x = 0.3 due to phase boundaries hindering domain-wall movement, before falling back at x = 0.5.. Mechanism: High saturation magnetization in FCC structures is attributed to higher atomic packing density (more ferromagnetic atoms per unit volume) and the absence of anti-parallel magnetic coupling elements like Cr; electrical resistivity increases due to lattice distortion from Al/Si, chemical randomness acting as point defects, and electron scattering; mechanical strength and malleability are governed by the phase composition (FCC favors plasticity, BCC increases lattice resistance) and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortion.. Limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.4, ductility diminishes and samples become brittle; the A8 alloy shatters immediately after elastic deformation; coercivity is highly sensitive to microstructure and difficult to predict solely from composition; ab initio calculations systematically overestimate saturation magnetization compared to experiments due to limited system size and ignored impurities/phase segregation.. Future work: The authors suggest that coercivity can be tuned within a wide range at a given composition by controlling quenching rates and applying heat/pressure treatments to further reduce Hc; the insights on composition-dependent structures and properties can guide the design of structural and functional HEAs and the development of high-entropy soft magnetic materials.. Quote: "the optimal balance of magnetic, electrical, and mechanical properties is achieved at x = 0.2, for which the combination of saturation magnetization (1.15 T), coercivity (1,400 A/m), electrical resistivity (69.5 μΩ·cm), yield strength (342 MPa), and strain without fracture (50%) makes the alloy an excellent SMM."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the change in deformation mechanism from crystallographic slip at room temperature to transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) at cryogenic temperatures impact the magnetic and electrical properties of the Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 high entropy alloy?. System: Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10 (at%) high entropy alloy. Processing: Arc-melted from pure elements (>99.5 wt.%), homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, solution heat treated at 900 °C for 1 h followed by oil quenching; tensile deformation applied at 298 K (RT) and 77 K (LN) to ~22% plastic strain at a strain rate of ≈ 4 × 10–1 s−1. Test conditions: Magnetic measurements performed in a cryogenic physical property measurement system (2–350 K) with fields up to 9 T; resistivity measured via four-point method; EBSD and XRD used for phase and strain analysis. Findings: Yield strength increased from ~150 MPa at RT to 340 MPa at LN (≈130% increase).; HCP phase fraction increased from 0% to 66% following 22.5% plastic strain at 77 K.; Magnetic moment dropped significantly for deformed specimens compared to undeformed (e.g., 0.4 emu/g at 0.05 T vs 1.8 emu/g at 9 T for undeformed at 2 K).; Coercive fields for deformed samples were ~60% larger than undeformed samples (108–78 gauss for undeformed).; Residual resistivity increased by ~10% for RT deformed and ~25% for LN deformed samples.; An abrupt increase in magnetization at 70 K for the undeformed sample was smeared out in deformed samples.; The system exhibits a ferrimagnetic ground state with coexisting antiferromagnetic phase, evidenced by non-saturating magnetization up to 9 T.. Mechanism: The deformation-induced FCC-to-HCP transformation and increased defect density (dislocations, stacking faults) enhance antiferromagnetic coupling between Mn/Cr and Fe/Co moments, leading to reduced bulk magnetization, smeared magnetic transitions, and increased coercivity due to domain wall pinning by defects and residual stresses.. Limitations: The magnetic ordering temperatures were not established due to limitations in the experimental setup (Tc exceeding 350 K); defect densities were not quantified; directional dependence of magnetic properties exists due to large grain size (200–250 μm).. Future work: Further investigation is needed to quantify defect densities and their specific impact on magnetic ground states; the study suggests that structural phase and defect density must both be considered to define physical properties.. Quote: "Plastic deformation was accommodated via crystallographic slip at room temperature while transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) has been observed in samples deformed at 77 K."

Question: What is the origin of the superior strength and plasticity in the CrCoNi alloy compared to the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, and how do magnetic properties influence the phase stability between fcc and hcp structures?. System: CrCoNi (ternary), CrMnFeCoNi (quinary), FeCoNi, MnCoNi, MnFeNi (equiatomic ternary derivatives). Processing: Alloys prepared as single-phase fcc solid solutions; samples deformed to approximately 55% true strain; DFT calculations using VASP with GGA-PBE, quasi-harmonic approximation for vibrational entropy, and special quasi-random structures (SQS); atomistic simulations using classical potentials on fcc Co as a surrogate.. Test conditions: Cryogenic to room temperature regimes relevant to experiments; shear deformations inducing stacking faults and twin interfaces; magnetic and non-magnetic DFT calculations; atomic resolution STEM in HAADF mode along 110 and 101 zone axes.. Findings: CrCoNi exhibits a distinctly lower-energy hcp phase compared to fcc at low temperatures, driven by vibrational entropy, whereas CrMnFeCoNi shows negligible energy difference due to magnetic frustration.; In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is favored over fcc even when magnetic effects are turned off, while in Mn-containing alloys (MnCoNi, MnFeNi), magnetism reduces the energy difference between phases to nearly zero.; Mn atoms exhibit magnetic frustration with moments fluctuating between approximately 3 and -3 μB regardless of environment, unlike Cr moments which show a narrower distribution and stronger dependence on local chemistry.; The average stacking fault energy in CrCoNi is negative, indicating a driving force for fcc-to-hcp transformation, whereas in CrMnFeCoNi, energy overlaps between stable and unstable structures prevent a clear driving force.; Hcp laths in CrCoNi form localized to stacking faults and twin interfaces via the glide of 1/6<112> Shockley partial dislocations, rather than as a bulk transformation.; Dislocation interactions with twin boundaries in CrCoNi lead to the nucleation of 3-layer hcp structures, which act as barriers to slip while redirecting shear to prevent stress concentration.; The hcp phase in CrCoNi can heal back to fcc upon removal of stress or interaction with intersecting slip systems, allowing for recovery without loss of plasticity.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the superior mechanical properties of CrCoNi arise from a magnetically-driven fcc-to-hcp phase transformation triggered by dislocation slip. In CrCoNi, the hcp phase is intrinsically lower in energy (ground state) at low temperatures, and the absence of magnetic frustration allows this transformation to proceed readily at stacking faults and twin boundaries. This creates nanostructured hcp laths that strengthen the material by blocking dislocations while simultaneously redirecting shear to avoid crack initiation. In contrast, the addition of Mn in CrMnFeCoNi introduces magnetic frustration, which eliminates the energy difference between fcc and hcp phases, suppressing the transformation and resulting in inferior mechanical performance.. Limitations: Free energy calculations for the quinary CrMnFeCoNi alloy pose significant practical challenges and yielded non-conclusive estimates; the study uses fcc Co as a surrogate system for atomistic simulations of dislocation interactions in CrCoNi due to the lack of reliable interatomic potentials for the Ni-Co-Cr system.. Future work: The authors suggest that new alloying combinations can be predicted based on favorable magnetic properties to design single-phase alloys with metastable structures, emphasizing that high-entropy alloys with more constituent elements are not necessarily superior to their derivatives.. Quote: "This highlights the unique combination of chemistry and magnetic properties in CrCoNi, leading to a fcc-hcp phase transformation that occurs only in this alloy."

W2126872936.title: Physical Properties of High Entropy Alloys

W2808754086.title: Ab initio phase stabilities and mechanical properties of multicomponent alloys: A comprehensive review for high entropy alloys and compositionally complex alloys

card: Paper card. Question: How do the type and number of elements in Ni-based single-phase equiatomic alloys affect their electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, particularly regarding the role of chemical and magnetic disorder?. System: Eight Ni-based FCC equiatomic alloys: elemental Ni, NiCo, NiFe, NiCoFe, NiCoCr, NiCoFeCr, NiCoFeCrMn, and NiCoFeCrPd. Processing: Arc-melting of pure elemental metals (>99.9% pure) followed by five flips and re-melts, drop-casting into a copper mold, and conversion to single crystals or polycrystalline rods via optical floating zone furnace; samples cut to ~1 × 1 × 10 mm3 and electrolytically polished. Test conditions: Electrical resistivity and thermal conductivity measured from 4 to 300 K; magnetization measured in magnetic fields up to 4 T from 4 to 300 K. Findings: Resistivities of alloys containing Cr (e.g., NiCoCr, NiCoFeCr) are about one order of magnitude larger than those without Cr (e.g., NiCoFe, NiFe).; The residual resistivity does not strongly correlate with the number of elements; the addition of Cr rapidly increases resistivity while Co has limited effects.; Thermal conductivities of the alloys are largely lower than pure metals primarily because high electrical resistivity suppresses the electronic thermal conductivity.; In concentrated alloys, lattice thermal conductivity (κg) dominates at low temperatures and is comparable to electronic thermal conductivity (κe) at room temperature.; The NiCoFeCrMn alloy exhibits a resistivity minimum at ~25 K, suggesting Kondo-like behavior or a spin glass transition.; NiCoCr is paramagnetic above 4 K, while NiCoFeCr has a Curie temperature (Tc) of ~120 K.; The addition of Cr significantly reduces magnetization due to magnetic cancellation, as Cr moments are anti-parallel to Ni, Co, and Fe moments.. Mechanism: High residual resistivity in alloys containing Cr and Mn is strongly attributed to magnetic disorder, where the presence of antiferromagnetically coupled elements (Cr, Mn) alongside ferromagnetically coupled elements (Ni, Co, Fe) creates strong scattering potentials for both spin-up and spin-down electrons, shortening the electron mean-free-path.. Limitations: The KKR-CPA calculations neglect displacement fluctuations, which may contribute to residual resistivity, particularly in alloys with large atomic size mismatches like NiCoFeCrPd.. Future work: Further studies are needed to investigate the origin of the finite positive TCR at low temperatures in NiCoCr, and additional experiments (ac susceptibility, heat capacity, neutron scattering) are required to conclusively determine the nature of the transition near 25 K in NiCoFeCrMn.. Quote: "The scattering of electrons is significantly increased due to the chemical (especially magnetic) disorder."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the application of a strong static magnetic field (SSMF) during solidification influence the microstructure evolution and the mechanical, electrical, and magnetic properties of FeCoNi(AlSi)0.2 high-entropy alloy?. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)0.2 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Arc-melting under argon atmosphere followed by re-melting four times; samples vacuum-sealed in quartz tubes and solidified using a self-built 8-Tesla facility with heating rates of 0.3 °C/s to 1450 °C (held 1 h), cooling at 1 °C/s to ~1200 °C, and water quenching; magnetic field intensities applied at 0T, 1T, 3T, 5T, and 7T.. Test conditions: Room temperature compression tests (strain rate 5 × 10−4 s−1), Vickers hardness (200 g load, 15 s hold), four-probe resistivity measurement, and hysteresis loop testing via VSM at room temperature.. Findings: Vickers hardness increases then decreases with magnetic field intensity, reaching a maximum of 190 HV (parallel) and 187 HV (perpendicular) at 5T.; Yield strength decreases then increases, reaching a minimum of 172 MPa at 5T.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) reaches a maximum of 121.7 emu/g (vertical) and 97.7 emu/g (parallel) at 5T.; Coercivity (Hc) reaches a minimum of 2.19 Oe (vertical) and 2.29 Oe (parallel) at 5T.; Electrical resistivity continuously increases with magnetic field intensity, reaching a maximum of 110 μΩ·cm at 7T.; A minor body-centered-cubic (BCC) phase precipitates in the perpendicular direction at 7T, while the alloy remains a single FCC phase up to 5T.; The volume fraction of dendritic phase is smallest at 5T, while the interdendritic phase volume fraction is largest at 5T.. Mechanism: The magnetic field influences microstructure evolution (phase species, volume fraction, and crystal orientation), atomic-level structure, and defect density (vacancies and dislocations). The increase in resistivity is attributed to 'frozen' vacancies from quenching and increased dislocation density induced by the magnetic field. The variation in saturation magnetization is attributed to the magnetic field's effect on atomic-level structure, while coercivity changes are linked to grain size, grain boundary density, and the presence of the BCC phase at 7T.. Limitations: The specific influence mechanism of the magnetic field on the atomic-level structure requires further study. The discontinuous change in resistivity and abnormal magnetic properties at 7T related to the precipitated BCC phase need verification by further experiments.. Future work: Further experiments are needed to verify the relationship between the precipitated BCC phase and the discontinuous changes in resistivity and magnetic properties at 7T, as well as to study the specific influence mechanism of the magnetic field on the atomic-level structure.. card: Paper card. Question: Can a varying stress-field ramping (VS-FR) loading sequence reduce the magnetic field levels required for complete reversible martensitic transformation in NiCoMnIn meta-magnetic shape memory alloys to below 2 T, and how does microstructure influence this requirement?. System: Ni44.8Co5.0Mn36.0In14.1 at.% single crystals (nominal Ni45Co5Mn36.6In13.4), specifically comparing Solution Heat Treated (SHT) and Secondary Annealed (SHT + 873 K 30 min) conditions.. Processing: Vacuum induction melting of high purity constituents; single crystal growth via Bridgman method under He; Solution Heat Treatment (SHT) at 1173 K for 24 hours followed by water quench; Secondary annealing at 873 K for 30 min followed by water quench; samples cut to 4 mm × 4 mm × 8 mm with [001] austenite orientation.. Test conditions: Isothermal constant stress and stress-varying magnetic field ramping; temperatures of 263 K (SHT) and 291 K (SHT+873K); strain rate of 2.5 · 10−5 s−1; magnetic field ramp rate ≤ 50 Oe s−1; field applied collinear to stress along [001] direction.. Findings: The SHT sample achieved complete martensite to austenite transformation under only 1.3 T applied magnetic field.; The SHT + 873 K 30 min sample required 3 T to achieve complete transformation using the VS-FR sequence.; The VS-FR sequence reduced magnetic hysteresis from 4 T (in CS-FR) to nearly zero for the secondary annealed sample.; Entropy changes of 14.7 J kg−1 K−1 (SHT) and 22 J kg−1 K−1 (SHT+873K) were generated under low fields.; Transformation strain reached 5.35% for SHT and 5.59% for SHT+873K under magnetic field ramping.; The Clausius-Clapeyron slope was 2.2 MPa K−1 for SHT and 3.16 MPa K−1 for SHT+873K.; The SHT sample exhibited a transformation hardening of 7 MPa, while the SHT+873K sample showed 27 MPa.; The transition range (Ms − Mf) was 22 K for SHT and 50 K for SHT+873K.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the lower field requirement in the SHT sample to smaller transformation hardening and a narrower transition range, caused by smaller L21 morphology (≤30 nm) without clear anti-phase boundaries (APBs). In contrast, the secondary annealed sample has large L21 domains separated by APBs which act as pinning sites for martensite propagation, increasing hardening and requiring higher fields. The VS-FR process minimizes magnetic hysteresis by applying and removing the magnetic field under different stress levels, effectively lowering the energy barrier for transformation.. Limitations: The exact correlation between martensite crystal structure dependence on austenite ordering is not fully understood, and the specific link between transformation hardening, crystallographic order, and martensite variant size scales requires more work.. Future work: The authors state that the reasons for the difference in entropy change between the two microstructures will be discussed in future works, and that designing a solid-state refrigerator applying the VS-FR loading sequence will be the topic of a follow-up publication.. Quote: "The complete martensite to austenite transformation was achieved with only 1.3 T in Ni45Co5Mn36.6In13.4 (at.%) single crystals."

card: Paper card. Question: How do axial magnetic fields affect the morphology, total volume, and transverse section area of the primary Al2Cu phase during the directional solidification of hypereutectic Al-Cu alloys, and what is the underlying mechanism involving thermoelectric magnetic forces?. System: Hypereutectic Al-40 wt.%Cu alloy. Processing: Directional solidification using a Bridgman type furnace with an upward thermal gradient of 6000 K/m and a constant pulling speed of 2 μm/s, under axial magnetic fields of 0T, 6T, 10T, and 12T provided by a superconductor magnet.. Test conditions: Axial magnetic fields ranging from 0 to 14T; solidification in a corundum crucible (3 mm inner diameter) sealed in an argon atmosphere; 3D quantification via synchrotron X-ray tomography (53 KeV beam, 1.3 × 1.3 μm2 pixel size); dislocation analysis via transmission electron microscope.. Findings: The total volume of the primary Al2Cu phase increases with rising magnetic field intensity.; The transverse section area of each Al2Cu column gradually decreases as the magnetic field increases, indicating refinement.; At 12T, the non-faceted feature of the Al2Cu phase becomes dominating, whereas 90° angles (faceted) are typical without a field.; A torque forms on the Al2Cu column due to thermoelectric magnetic forces (TEMF), causing fragmentation of the continuously grown column.; Strong stresses up to 3.3 × 10^8 N/m^2 are generated in the Al2Cu column by TEMF.; Samples solidified under a 10T magnetic field show a number of dislocations, while those without the field are nearly dislocation-free.; The degree of refinement and growth enhancement increases linearly with the applied magnetic field flux intensity.. Mechanism: The authors attribute refinement to the fragmentation of the Al2Cu column caused by a torque generated by thermoelectric magnetic forces (TEMF) acting on the solid. Growth enhancement is attributed to TEMF-induced dislocation multiplication, which provides more vacancies for atom attachment, thereby facilitating the growth of the faceted phase. The linear increase in effects is explained by the linear proportionality of TEMF to the magnetic field flux intensity.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work proposed by the authors.. Quote: "With rising magnetic fields, both increase of Al2Cu phase's total volume and decrease of each column's transverse section area were found."

card: Paper card. Question: How do strong homogeneous and gradient magnetic fields affect the nucleation behavior, undercooling, and recalescence of a highly undercooled Co76Sn24 near-eutectic alloy?. System: Co76Sn24 (at. %) near-eutectic alloy with B2O3 glass slag flux. Processing: Cold crucible levitation melting to prepare ingots, followed by glass slag fluxing in a quartz tube crucible inside a 12 T superconducting magnet; heating/cooling rates controlled by furnace; homogeneous field (12 T) and gradient field (93 T/m) applied during cooling. Test conditions: Temperature range up to 1437 K; homogeneous magnetic field of 12 T; gradient magnetic field of 93 T/m (field intensity at sample position 6.23 T); cyclic heating; undercooling measured via two-color pyrometer (50 Hz); magnetic force monitored via electronic balance. Findings: Mean undercooling without magnetic field is 246 K, remaining unchanged at 245 K under 12 T homogeneous field.; Mean undercooling decreases to 232 K under a 93 T/m gradient magnetic field (a reduction of 14 K).; Recalescence extent (ΔT R-N) decreases from 177 K (0 T) to 134 K (12 T homogeneous field) in the first 10 cycles.; Recalescence extent increases from 177 K (0 T) to 194 K under 93 T/m gradient magnetic field.; Calculated magnetic Gibbs free energy (ΔG M) is 28 J/mol, only ~1% of the chemical Gibbs free energy (ΔH f = 13.027 kJ/mol).; Volume fraction of anomalous eutectics formed during recalescence is 95.8% (0 T), 96.4% (12 T), and 99.5% (gradient field).; The undercooled melt remains in a paramagnetic state down to the nucleation temperature (1152 K).; The magnetic force exerted on the sample in the gradient field is approximately 17 times the sample's weight.. Mechanism: The magnetic field has a negligible effect on nucleation thermodynamics because the magnetic Gibbs free energy is only ~1% of the chemical driving force. In homogeneous fields, the unchanged undercooling is due to this weak thermodynamic effect, while the reduced recalescence is attributed to magnetic-field-induced defects (dislocations, vacancies) storing energy. In gradient fields, the paramagnetic melt experiences a strong downward compressive force that alters the sample shape, disrupts the equilibrium with the glass slag, and weakens the slag's purifying effect, thereby reducing undercooling; the increased recalescence is due to a higher volume fraction of solidification during the rapid release of latent heat.. Limitations: The authors state it is not easy to undercool the Co-Sn alloy below its liquid Curie temperature with the present technique, which limits the observation of magnetic contributions to nucleation temperature. The effect of magnetic field on the heating/cooling kinetics was found to be very limited.. Quote: "The mean undercooling of the undercooled melt is not altered by homogeneous magnetic field but depressed by gradient magnetic field."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the structural, magnetic, and transport properties of the new equimolar high-entropy alloy FeRhIrPdPt, and how do its dual-phase microstructure and constituent binary alloys explain its magnetic behavior?. System: FeRhIrPdPt (equimolar), FeRh4, FeIr4, FePd4, FePt4. Processing: Arc melting of constituent elements (Fe, Rh, Ir, Pd, Pt) with 99.9% purity in an Ar atmosphere to form 1.5 g button-shaped samples, followed by quenching on a water-chilled Cu hearth and multiple remelting cycles for homogeneity; no heat treatment or deformation applied.. Test conditions: XRD with Cu-Kα radiation; SEM/EDX at room temperature; DC magnetic susceptibility (χdc) between 50–450 K and 2 K; AC magnetic susceptibility (χac) between 3–300 K at frequencies 20 Hz–5 kHz; Electrical resistivity (ρ) between 3–300 K using a dc four-probe method.. Findings: The alloy forms a dual-phase fcc structure with a Rh- and Ir-rich main phase (70 vol.%) and a Pd- and Pt-rich minor phase (30 vol.%).; The main phase is responsible for a canonical spin-glass transition at approximately 90 K.; The minor phase is responsible for a ferromagnetic correlation that appears below 300 K.; FeRh4 and FeIr4 binary alloys exhibit spin-freezing behavior, while FePd4 and FePt4 are ferromagnetic with Curie temperatures of ~400 K and ~317 K, respectively.; The effective magnetic moment (μeff) for FeRhIrPdPt is 3.40 μB/Fe, with a positive Weiss temperature (ΘCW) of 308 K indicating FM correlation.; The Mydosh parameter K for FeRhIrPdPt is 0.007, classifying it as a canonical spin-glass HEA.; Electrical resistivity of FeRhIrPdPt slightly increases on cooling, indicating weak carrier localization, unlike the metallic behavior of the binary alloys.; The dual-phase formation is explained by the pairwise formation enthalpies, where Fe-Pd and Fe-Pt pairings are more robust than Fe-Rh and Fe-Ir.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the dual-phase microstructure results from the thermodynamic preference for specific binary pairings (Fe-Pd, Fe-Pt, Ir-Rh) based on negative formation enthalpies. The magnetic properties arise from the independent contributions of the two phases: the Rh/Ir-rich main phase (analogous to FeRh4/FeIr4) drives the spin-glass transition at 90 K, while the Pd/Pt-rich minor phase (analogous to FePd4/FePt4) drives the ferromagnetic correlation below 300 K. The lack of long-range ordering in the ferromagnetic correlation is attributed to the inhomogeneous magnetic state of the minor phase.. Limitations: The study was limited to as-cast samples without heat treatment or deformation; the thermal stability of the dual-phase microstructure was not investigated.. Future work: The authors state it is important to understand the thermal stability of the alloy to control the microstructure, and to investigate the possibility of multifunctional magnetic properties where the two phases offer different functions.. Quote: "The dual-phase is composed of a Rh- and Ir-rich main phase and a Pd- and Pt-rich minor one."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the miscibility gap in bimetallic Co-Mo alloys be overcome to create tunable, highly active catalysts for ammonia decomposition using earth-abundant elements?. System: Quinary CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 where x + y = 70) and control samples of bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru. Processing: Carbothermal shock technique involving flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon nanofibers; temperature reached 2000–2300 K with ramping rates on the order of 10^5 K s−1 and shock duration of ~55 ms. Test conditions: Ammonia decomposition in a plug flow reactor at 250–600 °C using 5 vol% NH3 (and 100 vol% NH3 for specific tests) at a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 36 L gcat−1 h−1. Findings: HEA-Co25Mo45 achieved a mass-specific reaction rate of 22.1 gNH3 gmetals−1 h−1 at 500 °C, representing an improvement factor of ~19 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~3 versus Ru.; The most active catalyst, HEA-Co25Mo45, reached 50% NH3 conversion (T50) at 422 °C, compared to 600 °C for Ru and 600 °C for bimetallic Co-Mo.; The apparent activation energy (Eapp) varied from 64.7 kJ mol−1 for the most active HEA-Co25Mo45 to 123.1 kJ mol−1 for the least active HEA-Co55Mo15.; Nitrogen desorption energy (ΔEN) for HEA-Co25Mo45 was ~79 kJ mol−1, which is very close to the value for Ru (84 kJ mol−1).; Catalytic activity exhibited a volcano-type behavior with respect to nitrogen adsorption energy, peaking at an optimal ΔEN of ~79 kJ mol−1.; The HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst showed negligible degradation after ~50 hours of continuous operation at 500 °C.; For pure NH3 decomposition, HEA-Co55Mo15 achieved an improvement factor of ~118 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~40 versus Ru.; Atomistic modeling confirmed a single solid-solution phase with δ = 5.4% and ΔHmix = 0.65 kJ mol−1, showing no phase segregation up to 1000 K.. Mechanism: The high catalytic activity is attributed to the robust tuning of surface nitrogen binding strength via the Co/Mo ratio; the optimal activity arises from a tradeoff where Co-rich catalysts bind N too weakly (limiting dehydrogenation) and Mo-rich catalysts bind N too strongly (limiting N2 desorption), with the HEA composition allowing access to the optimal intermediate binding energy (~79 kJ mol−1) predicted by the Sabatier principle.. Limitations: The text notes that the peak intensities in XRD patterns are low due to the much smaller particle sizes compared to previously reported HEAs, and that the bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts are constrained by large miscibility gaps in their phase diagram.. Future work: The authors propose designing practical reactors with cascaded catalyst layers having gradually changing nitrogen binding strengths to match the varying concentration of NH3 along the flow, which can be readily achieved by varying the Co/Mo ratios in HEA catalysts.. Quote: "Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram."
