card: Paper card. Question: How does dendritic liquation during casting influence the spatial formation of martensite crystals in TiZrHfCoNiCu versus CoNiCuAlGaIn high entropy shape memory alloys?. System: Ti16.67Zr16.67Hf16.67Co10Ni25Cu15 and Co31.22Ni29.26Cu11.95Al16.64Ga10.39In0.55. Processing: Arc-melting from high-purity elements (iodide Ti, Zr, Hf; electrolytic Co, Ni, Cu; Al, Ga, In) in pre-gettered argon; ingots turned and re-melted nine times; weight 5–10 g; DTA heating/cooling rates of 40 K min−1. Test conditions: Room temperature SEM imaging; DTA measurements with ±7K accuracy; EDX line scans across dendritic and interdendritic regions. Findings: TiZrHfCoNiCu crystallization starts at 1530 K with a peak width of 120 K, while CoNiCuAlGaIn starts at 1500 K with a peak width of 174 K.; In Ti16.67Zr16.67Hf16.67Co10Ni25Cu15, martensite crystals fill the dendrites, whereas in Co31.22Ni29.26Cu11.95Al16.64Ga10.39In0.55, they form only in interdendritic regions.; The crystallization temperature for Ti16.67Zr16.67Hf16.67Co10Ni25Cu15 is 1250 K, with a peak width of 164 K, compared to 1587 K and 65 K for binary TiNi.; Martensite crystals in Co31.22Ni29.26Cu11.95Al16.64Ga10.39In0.55 stop at the boundary of dendrites, with a 20-μm long crystal staying entirely within the interdendritic region.; The correlation coefficient between enthalpy and entropy of mixing is −0.87 for TiZrHfCoNiCu, while for CoNiCuAlGaIn, enthalpy of mixing correlates with Cu concentration at 0.99.; Dendrite regions in TiZrHfCoNiCu show the highest entropy of mixing (14.61 Jmol−1K−1) and atomic size difference, correlating with martensite formation.; Interdendritic regions in TiZrHfCoNiCu are stabilized against martensitic transformation due to lower negative enthalpy of mixing and lower entropy of mixing.. Mechanism: Martensite crystals form in regions with higher lattice distortion (higher atomic size difference and entropy of mixing) and propagate through these highly distorted areas but cannot penetrate less distorted regions where diffusional phase transformations (precipitation) stabilize the austenite phase.. Limitations: Strong dendritic liquation leads to chemical inhomogeneities and precipitates (e.g., Ti2Ni-like phases) that degrade shape memory behavior upon fatigue; simple solution treatments cannot fully avoid these precipitations.. Future work: Control of crystallization parameters to refine microstructures for cast and ready-to-use HESMA without subsequent solutionizing, particularly for 3D printing applications.. Quote: "In contrast, in the CoNiCuAlGaIn system the dendritic liquation allows the martensite crystals to form only in interdendritic regions."

card: Paper card. Question: Can single-source precursors be used to synthesize metastable fcc-structured refractory binary alloys that lie within miscibility gaps, and how do their compressibility and structural stability compare to ideal solution models under high pressure?. System: fcc–Ir0.50Pt0.50, fcc–Rh0.66Pt0.33, fcc–Rh0.50Pd0.50; precursors: [Ir(NH3)5Cl][PtCl6], [Ir(NH3)5Cl][PtBr6], [Rh(NH3)5Cl]2[PtCl6]Cl2, [Rh(NH3)5Cl][PdCl4]·H2O. Processing: Thermal decomposition of single-source precursors in gaseous hydrogen flow at temperatures below 800 °C (specifically 400–700 °C depending on the precursor); precursors synthesized from aqueous solutions at room temperature.. Test conditions: Room temperature compression up to 50 GPa in diamond anvil cells using Helium as a pressure transmitting medium; X-ray diffraction at ID15B beamline (λ = 0.411235 Å).. Findings: fcc–Ir0.50Pt0.50 and fcc–Rh0.50Pd0.50 are metastable alloys corresponding to miscibility gaps on binary metallic phase diagrams.; fcc–Ir0.50Pt0.50 has an atomic volume V0/Z = 14.597(6) Å3·atom−1, bulk modulus B0 = 321(6) GPa, and B0' = 6(1).; fcc–Rh0.66Pt0.33 has an atomic volume V0/Z = 14.211(3) Å3·atom−1, bulk modulus B0 = 259(1) GPa, and B0' = 6.66(9).; fcc–Rh0.50Pd0.50 has an atomic volume V0/Z = 14.18(2) Å3·atom−1, bulk modulus B0 = 223(4) GPa, and B0' = 5.0(3).; All investigated fcc-structured binary alloys are stable under compression up to 50 GPa with no pressure-induced phase transitions.; Atomic volumes and bulk moduli show good agreement with the ideal solutions model for most alloys.; Thermal decomposition of [Ir(NH3)5Cl][PtBr6] in inert atmosphere forms IrBr3 as an intermediate, leading to two-phase mixtures, unlike hydrogen flow which yields single-phase alloys.. Mechanism: The authors propose that thermal decomposition in hydrogen flow allows for the formation of single-phase alloys even within miscibility gaps, whereas inert atmospheres lead to two-phase mixtures due to the formation of metal bromide intermediates (e.g., IrBr3) that decompose differently. The compressibility behavior is explained by the alloys acting as ideal solid solutions, where atomic volumes and bulk moduli follow linear or predictable concentration dependencies.. Limitations: The text notes that fcc–Ir0.50Pt0.50 and fcc–Pt0.33Rh0.67 show large deviations from the ideal solutions model, and the deviation for fcc–Ir0.50Pt0.50 may be explained by relatively low experimental pressure, while the deviation for fcc–Pt0.33Rh0.67 requires further theoretical study.. Future work: The authors suggest that the mentioned large deviation from the ideal solutions model should be further studied theoretically and that diverse single-source precursors should be designed to prepare useful functional alloys as nanostructured powders for catalytic applications.. Quote: "Fcc–Ir0.50Pt0.50 and fcc–Rh0.50Pd0.50 correspond to miscibility gaps on binary metallic phase diagrams and can be considered as metastable alloys."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the influence of a hierarchically decomposed B2 + A2 structure on the formation of magnetic vortex states and the origin of coercivity in AlCo(Cr)FeNi high-entropy alloys?. System: AlCoFeNi and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi high-entropy alloys. Processing: Arc melting of Al, Co, Cr, Fe, and Ni pellets in an Ar atmosphere, followed by annealing at 600°C for 15 h in an Ar atmosphere and quenching in water. Test conditions: Bulk magnetization measured at 300 K up to 1 T; Lorentz TEM and off-axis electron holography performed in magnetic-field-free conditions and with applied out-of-plane fields up to 1.5 T; APT conducted at 60 K. Findings: AlCoFeNi has a saturation magnetization (MS) of 99.8 Am2/kg and coercivity (Hc) of 1.45 mT, while AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi has MS of 46.2 Am2/kg and Hc of 9.56 mT.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi exhibits a hierarchical structure with coarse A2 gen-1 (1–5 μm), medium A2 gen-2 (50-150 nm), and fine A2 gen-3 (<10 nm) phases in a B2 matrix.; A2 gen-2 precipitates in region R1 contain 3D magnetic vortex states with a magnetic induction peak of 0.5 ± 0.1 T.; The ratio of clockwise to counterclockwise magnetic vortices in A2 gen-2 precipitates is approximately 1:1 at remanence.; The A2 shell surrounding A2 gen-2 precipitates is 2 nm thick and has ~25% higher magnetization than the A2 gen-1 matrix in region R2.; Magnetic vortices in A2 gen-2 precipitates can reverse their rotation direction when exposed to external magnetic fields of 100–500 mT.; The B2 matrix in region R1 is weakly ferromagnetic and reverses its magnetization sign during magnetic switching.. Mechanism: The increased coercivity in AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi is attributed to a complex magnetization process involving the successive reversal of magnetic vortices within A2 precipitates and interactions with a weakly ferromagnetic B2 matrix, rather than simple domain wall pinning.. Limitations: The interactions between different magnetic elements remain unclear; off-axis electron holography cannot detect the magnetic vortex core direction; the study does not cover the effects of temperature, strain, or magnetic field on precipitate formation.. Future work: Future studies should determine the effect of external magnetic field and/or stress annealing, kinetics, and other external stimuli on precipitate formation to control magnetic anisotropy and properties; in situ magnetizing experiments and micromagnetic simulations are needed to address dynamic reversal processes.. Quote: "We reveal for the first time the influence of a hierarchically decomposed B2 + A2 structure in an AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi HEA on the formation of magnetic vortex states within individual A2 (disordered BCC) precipitates."

W1997009546.title: Electron tomography and holography in materials science

card: Paper card. Question: How does the number of principal elements (N) in equimolar multi-principal element alloys affect the probability of forming disordered solid solution (SS) phases versus intermetallic (IM) phases, and what are the implications for high-temperature structural applications?. System: Equimolar combinations of 3 to 6 elements from a palette of 26 metallic elements (including Al, Si, Mo, Ta, W, Nb, Ti, V, Re, Zr, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, etc.). Processing: High-throughput computational screening using the CALPHAD method (Pandat v.8.1 software) to calculate phase diagrams for 134,547 equimolar alloy systems; results filtered for credibility where the fraction of fully assessed binary systems (fAB) equals 1.. Test conditions: Phase diagrams calculated between 600 °C and 3,600 °C; properties evaluated at the solidus temperature (Tm) and at 600 °C; maximum use temperature (Tuse) estimated as the lowest of 0.8Tm or the last first-order phase reaction temperature below Tm.. Findings: The fraction of solid solution (SS) alloys decreases as the number of elements (N) increases: at Tm, 30% of 3-component alloys are SS, dropping to only 5% for 6-component alloys.; Configurational entropy rises slowly with N (as ln(N)), while the number of binary interactions increases rapidly (as (N/2)(N−1)), explaining why IM formation becomes more probable as N increases.; The maximum solidus temperature (Tm) decreases with N: 2,925 °C for 3-component, 2,754 °C for 4-component, 2,435 °C for 5-component, and 2,056 °C for 6-component alloys.; The maximum maximum use temperature (Tuse) decreases with N: 2,285 °C for 3-component, 1,846 °C for 4-component, 1,677 °C for 5-component, and 1,159 °C for 6-component alloys.; Only 3 out of 209 SS alloys with Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C are 6-component alloys, whereas 108 are 3-component alloys.; Extreme property values (highest/lowest density, modulus, cost) are achieved in ternary (3-component) alloys, while 6-component alloys show tighter property spreads.; 51 equimolar alloy systems with 3 ≤ N ≤ 5 were identified that satisfy aggressive design criteria (Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C, density ≤ 10 g cm−3, modulus ≥ 100 GPa, cost ≤ $200/kg, no IM phases at Tm).. Mechanism: The authors argue that while configurational entropy (Smix) favors solid solution stability, it increases only logarithmically with the number of elements. Conversely, the number of binary element pairs increases quadratically, raising the probability that at least one pair has a sufficiently large negative formation enthalpy (Hf) to overcome the entropy term in the Gibbs free energy equation (G = H - TS), thereby stabilizing intermetallic phases.. Limitations: The study is restricted to equimolar compositions; non-equimolar alloys were not explored and may offer higher Tm or Tuse values. Additionally, the credibility filter (fAB=1) excluded over 95% of the calculated systems, potentially missing viable alloys if less stringent criteria were acceptable.. Future work: The authors propose extending the screening to non-equimolar alloys to uncover local compositions with extreme properties, conducting more extensive experimental validations to potentially relax credibility criteria, and developing high-throughput experimental techniques capable of handling microstructural length scales.. Quote: "We find the surprising result that solid solution alloys become less likely as the number of alloy elements increases."

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-throughput first-principles calculations be utilized to predict temperature- and composition-dependent phase evolution in Al-containing high-entropy alloys, specifically regarding the formation of ordered multiphase microstructures?. System: AlxCoCrFeNi (where x ranges from 1 to 2) and Al1.3CoCrCuFeNi. Processing: High-throughput Monte Carlo simulations on a fixed BCC lattice using binary interaction energies derived from an enthalpy matrix; experimental validation via in situ neutron scattering (room temp to 1600°C using aerodynamic levitation), in situ STEM heating (room temp to 700°C), and DSC (cooling at 20°C/min from 1450 to 250°C). Test conditions: Simulations: cooling from high temperatures; Neutron scattering: 300 K to 1600°C; STEM: 300 K to 700°C; DSC: 1450°C to 250°C at 20°C/min. Findings: The ordering onset temperature (Tc) is strongly dependent on Al content, ranging from approximately 1220 °C for x = 1 to 1850 °C for x = 2.; In Al2CoCrFeNi (x=2), the B2 phase remains strongly ordered at the melting point, whereas in AlCoCrFeNi (x=1), B2 order is lost near 1400 °C.; A sharp transformation involving phase separation occurs near 600 °C for all compositions between x = 1 and 2.; Below 600 °C, the B2 phase is primarily composed of Ni, Co, and Al, while the disordered phase is primarily composed of Fe and Cr.; The fraction of Al-Al pairs decreases as Al content increases, indicating significant short-range order around Al atoms even in the high-temperature disordered BCC phase.; DSC measurements on AlCoCrFeNi show a peak near 575 °C, consistent with the simulated transformation temperature of 565 ± 30 °C.; In situ STEM reveals that Cr-Fe-enriched plate-like microstructures decompose upon heating to 600 °C, with complete breakdown into globular Cr-rich regions by 700 °C.. Mechanism: The phase evolution is driven by the strong ordering tendencies of Al with transition metals (particularly Ni and Co) leading to B2 formation, followed by a temperature-dependent separation where weakly interacting elements (Cr, Fe) precipitate into a disordered BCC solid solution while Al, Ni, and Co remain in the ordered B2 sublattices; this is modeled via nearest-neighbor interactions on a rigid lattice where configurational entropy decreases during cooling.. Limitations: The lattice-constrained simulations neglect the possibility of changing the underlying lattice and ignore potential vibrational entropy effects associated with small displacements from the average position; the limited length scales in simulations may prevent a full description of the behavior.. Future work: The approach provides a simple method to guide the development of ordered multi-phase HEAs for structural applications and suggests a broader strategy for rapid exploration of phase evolution where little experimental data exists.. Quote: "Using a simple model with parameters derived from first-principles calculations, we reproduce the major features associated with Al-containing phases"

card: Paper card. Question: How does the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, combined with annealing temperature, influence the hierarchical phase decomposition, microstructure, and resulting magnetic and mechanical properties in AlCoFeNi-based high entropy alloys?. System: AlCoFeNi (x=1) and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi (x=0.5) high entropy alloys. Processing: Arc melting of elemental pellets (99.9% purity) under argon atmosphere followed by isothermal annealing at 600 °C and 1000 °C for 15 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Annealing at 600 °C/15 h and 1000 °C/15 h; characterization via SEM, EBSD, TEM, APT, Vickers microhardness, and magnetic saturation/coercivity measurements. Findings: AlCoFeNi annealed at 1000 °C forms a single ordered B2 phase with a microhardness of 406 VHN and saturation magnetization of 112 emu/g.; AlCoFeNi annealed at 600 °C decomposes into a B2 + BCC mixture with a microhardness of 474 VHN.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi annealed at 1000 °C exhibits coarse B2 + BCC phase separation with grain boundary FCC phases.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi annealed at 600 °C shows a hierarchical microstructure with decomposition length scales ranging from ~3–5 nm (APT) to ~50–100 nm (TEM) to micron-scale lamellae.; The AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy annealed at 600 °C achieved the highest microhardness of 475 VHN.; Saturation magnetization of the Cr-containing alloy (AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi) is reduced by more than 50% compared to the Cr-free alloy due to the antiferromagnetic nature of Cr.; Coercivity decreases with increasing annealing temperature, dropping from 15 Oe at 600 °C to 4 Oe at 1000 °C for the AlCoFeNi alloy.; APT cluster analysis detected Cr-rich BCC precipitates with concentrations ranging from 16% to 74% depending on the generation scale.. Mechanism: The addition of Cr enhances phase separation due to the positive enthalpy of mixing in Fe-Cr, Co-Cr, and Ni-Cr systems, which creates miscibility gaps, whereas the Al-Cr system has a negative enthalpy of mixing favoring compound formation; the length scale of decomposition is controlled by the interplay of composition and annealing temperature.. Limitations: The thermodynamic model predicted an FCC phase in AlCoFeNi at 1000 °C which was not observed experimentally, likely due to a high nucleation barrier; the specific thermodynamic basis for Cr's influence on phase separation in these complex multi-component alloys requires further analysis beyond the scope of the paper.. Future work: Further detailed investigation is required to understand the relationship between B2 phase decomposition into a two-phase B2 + BCC microstructure and the resulting coercivity; the details of the thermodynamic basis underlying the influence of Cr on phase separation require analysis beyond the current scope.. Quote: "The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature."

card: Paper card. Question: How do cold rolling and subsequent annealing treatments at different temperatures (800, 900, and 1000 °C) affect the microstructural evolution, specifically the formation of B2 precipitates and recrystallization states, and how do these microstructures influence the tensile strength and ductility of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys?. System: Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (at.%). Processing: Melted via magnetic levitation induction at 1600 °C, homogenized at 1150 °C for 24 h, cold-rolled to ~70% thickness reduction, and annealed at 800, 900, or 1000 °C for 60 min followed by water cooling.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests performed at room temperature with a strain rate of 10−3/s; hardness measured with 200 g load and 15 s dwell time.. Findings: The 800 °C-annealed specimen exhibited a partially recrystallized microstructure with quasi ultra-fine grains (~0.9 ± 0.6 μm) and a yield strength of ~870 ± 1.6 MPa.; The 900 °C-annealed specimen showed full recrystallization with fine grains (~2.2 ± 1.6 μm) and a B2 precipitate volume fraction of ~2.2 ± 0.3%.; The 1000 °C-annealed specimen displayed grain coarsening (~7.2 ± 5.3 μm) and a reduced B2 precipitate volume fraction of ~0.6 ± 0.1%.; B2 precipitates along grain boundaries increased in size from ~198 ± 84 nm (800 °C) to ~263 ± 146 nm (1000 °C) while their volume fraction decreased.; Small, elongated B2 precipitates were aligned along deformation twins in the non-recrystallized region of the 800 °C-annealed specimen.; The 800 °C-annealed specimen maintained a high ductility of ~25.5 ± 2.4% despite the high strength.; Precipitation strengthening contributed only ~10.5% and ~9.1% to the yield strength in 900 °C- and 1000 °C-annealed specimens, respectively.; Grain boundary strengthening was identified as the main mechanism for strength enhancement in fully recrystallized specimens.. Mechanism: The superior strength in the 800 °C-annealed specimen is attributed to heterogeneous microstructures combining quasi ultra-fine recrystallized grains, non-recrystallized grains with high dislocation density and deformation twins, and B2 precipitates, which also generate significant back-stress during deformation. In fully recrystallized states, strength is primarily driven by grain boundary strengthening (Hall-Petch effect), while precipitation strengthening plays a weak or neglected role due to the semi-coherent nature and size of the B2 precipitates.. Limitations: The study notes that more detailed investigations are needed to determine the critical conditions for recrystallization onset/completion and B2 precipitation/dissolution quantitatively, and that the contribution of precipitation strengthening is associated with specific precipitate parameters that require further optimization.. Future work: More studies about the kinetics of B2 precipitation and dissolution should be conducted to understand the variation trend of the size and volume fraction with increasing the annealing temperature, and detailed investigations should be done to determine the critical conditions for recrystallization and B2 phase transitions.. Quote: "The yield strength and ultimate tensile strength in 800 °C-annealed specimen were raised as high as ~870 and ~1060 MPa and the ductility was maintained at ~26%."
